title: Step 1: Downloading Historical Ship Logbook Data from ICOADS
text:
This notebook explains how to download Matthew Maury’s historic ship logbook collection from the ICOADS (International Comprehensive Ocean-Atmosphere Data Set) archive. By the end, you’ll understand:

What ICOADS is and why it matters for historical research
What a “deck” is and why we want deck 701
How the download script works step by step
The IMMA1 fixed-width format used to store the data

Note: The full download takes several hours and downloads ~500MB. This notebook explains the process; you can run the script separately or use pre-built data files.



Matthew Fontaine Maury (1806-1873) was a US Navy officer who revolutionized maritime navigation and founded modern oceanography. After an injury ended his sea career, he became Superintendent of the US Naval Observatory where he had a brilliant insight: systematically collect and analyze ship logbooks.
Maury convinced ship captains worldwide to record standardized observations of wind, weather, currents, and sea conditions. By synthesizing thousands of logbooks, he created the first wind and current charts that dramatically reduced sailing times—sometimes by weeks!
His 1855 book “The Physical Geography of the Sea” is widely considered the first textbook of modern oceanography.



ICOADS (International Comprehensive Ocean-Atmosphere Data Set) is the world’s largest collection of historical ocean-atmosphere observations. Maintained by NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), it contains hundreds of millions of marine observations dating back to the 1600s.
The data is organized by deck number—a historical term from the punch card era. Each deck represents a distinct data collection:



Deck
Description




701
US Maury Collection (our focus!)


702
US Marine Meteorological Journals


704
US Merchant Marine Collection


720
UK Met Office Main Marine Data Bank



Deck 701 contains Maury’s original digitized logbook collection from 1795-1861.



Let’s walk through the download script (scripts/download_icoads_deck701.py) to understand how it works.


ICOADS data is organized by year and month. Each file is gzip-compressed and made available at a URL of the form https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/international-comprehensive-ocean-atmosphere/v3/archive/final-untrim/IMMA1_R3.1.-_{TEAR}-{MONTH}.jz

# The archive URL structure
BASE_URL = "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/international-comprehensive-ocean-atmosphere/v3/archive/final-untrim/"

# Example file for January 1840
example_file = "IMMA1_R3.1.0_1840-01.gz"
print(f"Full URL: {BASE_URL}{example_file}")

# For Maury's collection period (1795-1861), we need:
n_years = 1861 - 1795 + 1
n_files = n_years * 12
print(f"\nTotal files to download: {n_files} ({n_years} years × 12 months)")




ICOADS uses the IMMA1 (International Maritime Meteorological Archive) format—a fixed-width text format where each field occupies specific character positions.
Here’s a sample observation:
1840 1 1     3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685                                                           165 20673701 69 5 0 1
The following code block explains what each character grouping means:

# A sample IMMA1 record
sample_record = "1840 1 1     3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685                                                           165 20673701 69 5 0 1"

print("IMMA1 Core Section Fields (with values from sample record):")
print("=" * 70)

# All IMMA1 Core fields in order (108 characters total)
# Based on ICOADS R3.1 IMMA1 format specification
fields = [
    # Date/Time fields
    (0, 4, 'YR', 'Year'),
    (4, 6, 'MO', 'Month'),
    (6, 8, 'DY', 'Day'),
    (8, 12, 'HR', 'Hour (HHMM format, ÷100 for decimal)'),
    # Position fields
    (12, 17, 'LAT', 'Latitude (×100, signed)'),
    (17, 23, 'LON', 'Longitude (×100, subtract 360 if >180)'),
    # Record metadata
    (23, 25, 'IM', 'IMMA version'),
    (25, 27, 'ATTC', 'Attachment count'),
    # Time/position indicators
    (27, 28, 'TI', 'Time indicator'),
    (28, 29, 'LI', 'Latitude/longitude indicator'),
    (29, 30, 'DS', 'Direction of ship'),
    (30, 31, 'VS', 'Speed of ship'),
    # Ship identification
    (31, 33, 'NID', 'Night/day indicator'),
    (33, 35, 'II', 'ID indicator'),
    (35, 44, 'ID', 'Ship ID (9-char truncated name)'),
    (44, 46, 'C1', 'Country code'),
    # Ship course and speed
    (46, 49, 'DI', 'Direction indicator'),
    (49, 51, 'D', 'Direction (tens of degrees)'),
    (51, 53, 'WI', 'Wind direction indicator'),
    (53, 56, 'W', 'Wind direction (degrees)'),
    # Visibility and weather
    (56, 57, 'VI', 'Visibility indicator'),
    (57, 59, 'VV', 'Visibility'),
    (59, 61, 'WW', 'Present weather'),
    (61, 62, 'W1', 'Past weather'),
    # Pressure
    (62, 67, 'SLP', 'Sea level pressure (×10 hPa)'),
    (67, 68, 'A', 'Pressure tendency characteristic'),
    (68, 71, 'PPP', 'Pressure tendency (×10 hPa)'),
    # Temperature
    (71, 72, 'IT', 'Temperature indicator'),
    (72, 76, 'AT', 'Air temperature (×10 °C)'),
    (76, 77, 'WBTI', 'Wet bulb temp indicator'),
    (77, 81, 'WBT', 'Wet bulb temperature'),
    (81, 82, 'DPTI', 'Dew point temp indicator'),
    (82, 86, 'DPT', 'Dew point temperature'),
    # Sea surface temperature
    (86, 87, 'SI', 'SST measurement indicator'),
    (87, 91, 'SST', 'Sea surface temperature (×10 °C)'),
    # Cloud data
    (91, 92, 'N', 'Total cloud amount'),
    (92, 93, 'NH', 'Low cloud amount'),
    (93, 94, 'CL', 'Low cloud type'),
    (94, 95, 'HI', 'Cloud height indicator'),
    (95, 96, 'H', 'Cloud base height'),
    (96, 97, 'CM', 'Middle cloud type'),
    (97, 98, 'CH', 'High cloud type'),
    # Wave data
    (98, 100, 'WD', 'Wave direction'),
    (100, 102, 'WP', 'Wave period'),
    (102, 104, 'WH', 'Wave height'),
    # (Core ends at position 108; C1 attachment follows)
]

for start, end, abbr, description in fields:
    value = sample_record[start:end] if end <= len(sample_record) else ''
    # Only print fields that have non-blank values
    if value.strip():
        print(f"  {start:3}-{end:3}  {abbr:5}  '{value}'  {description}")

print("\n" + "=" * 70)
print("C1 Attachment (follows Core at position 108+):")
c1_fields = [
    (113, 118, 'UID', 'Unique record identifier'),
    (118, 121, 'DCK', 'Deck number (701 = Maury Collection)'),
    (121, 124, 'SID', 'Source ID'),
    (124, 126, 'PT', 'Platform type'),
]
for start, end, abbr, description in c1_fields:
    value = sample_record[start:end] if end <= len(sample_record) else ''
    if value.strip():
        print(f"  {start:3}-{end:3}  {abbr:5}  '{value}'  {description}")




The deck number is in the C1 attachment, which follows the core section. For ICOADS R3.1, the deck number is at positions 118-120:

def get_deck_number(line):
    """
    Extract the deck number (DCK) from an IMMA1 record.

    The deck number identifies which collection the record belongs to.
    Deck 701 = US Maury Collection
    """
    DCK_START = 118
    DCK_END = 121

    if len(line) < DCK_END:
        return None

    dck = line[DCK_START:DCK_END]

    # Verify it's a valid deck number (3 digits)
    if dck.isdigit():
        return dck

    return None

# Demonstrate with a real record
full_record = "1840 1 1     3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685                                                           165 20673701 69 5 0 1                  FFFFFF77AAAAAAAAAAAA     981500A2243102199 0 760786218400101  3701N 7357W"
deck = get_deck_number(full_record)
print(f"Deck number extracted: {deck}")
print(f"This is {'the Maury Collection!' if deck == '701' else 'a different collection'}")




For each monthly file, we download, decompress, and filter:

import gzip
import io

def demonstrate_filtering(lines):
    """
    Show how we filter IMMA1 records for deck 701.
    """
    deck701_count = 0
    other_decks = {}

    for line in lines:
        deck = get_deck_number(line)
        if deck == '701':
            deck701_count += 1
        elif deck:
            other_decks[deck] = other_decks.get(deck, 0) + 1

    return deck701_count, other_decks

# Simulate filtering results (representative numbers)
print("Filtering Process:")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
For each monthly file:

1. Download compressed .gz file from NOAA archive
2. Decompress in memory (gzip)
  3. Parse each line, extract deck number at position 118-120
  4. If deck == '701', write to output file
  5. Otherwise, skip the record

Typical results for a month in the 1840s:

- Total records in file: ~50,000
- Deck 701 (Maury) records: ~2,000 (4%)
  - Other decks: ~48,000 (96%)
""")




Here’s the core logic from scripts/download_icoads_deck701.py:

# Simplified version of the download function (don't run - just for illustration)
DOWNLOAD_CODE = '''
import gzip
import urllib.request

def download_and_filter_deck701(start_year=1795, end_year=1861, output_file='data/icoads_deck701_maury.imma'):
    """Download ICOADS IMMA1 files and filter for deck 701 records."""

    base_url = "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/international-comprehensive-ocean-atmosphere/v3/archive/final-untrim/"

    with open(output_file, 'w') as outf:
        for year in range(start_year, end_year + 1):
            for month in range(1, 13):
                filename = f"IMMA1_R3.1.0_{year}-{month:02d}.gz"
                url = base_url + filename

                try:
                    # Download compressed file
                    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60) as response:
                        compressed_data = response.read()

                    # Decompress and process
                    data = gzip.decompress(compressed_data).decode('utf-8', errors='replace')

                    for line in data.strip().split('\\n'):
                        # Check if this record is from deck 701
                        if len(line) > 120 and line[118:121] == '701':
                            outf.write(line + '\\n')

                except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
                    if e.code == 404:
                        print(f"No data for {year}-{month:02d}")
                    else:
                        raise
'''

print("Download Script Overview:")
print("=" * 60)
print(DOWNLOAD_CODE)





To actually download the data, it is certainly possible to use the associated notebook. But it is easier to run the full script in teh background. From the project root:
uv run python scripts/download_icoads_deck701.py
Options:

--start-year 1840 --end-year 1850: Download only a subset of years
-o custom_output.imma: Specify output file
-q: Quiet mode (suppress progress)

Expected output: - Time: Fifteen minutes to several hours (depends on network speed) - File: data/icoads_deck701_maury.imma (~567 MB) - Records: ~1.3 million Maury collection observations



The downloaded IMMA1 file is in a legacy fixed-width format. In the next notebook, we’ll convert it to Apache Parquet for efficient analysis:

37× compression: 567 MB → 15 MB
Selective column reading: Load only the fields you need
Native data types: Proper integers and floats instead of text

Deck 701 contains Maury’s original ship logbook collection (1795-1861)
IMMA1 is a fixed-width text format; the deck number is at positions 118-120
The download script filters ~50 million records down to ~1.3 million Maury records
This process takes hours but only needs to be done once

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
The ICOADS data contains individual ship observations—single points in time and space. But for analysis, we want voyages: connected sequences of observations representing a ship’s journey. This notebook explains Ben Schmidt’s algorithm for reconstructing voyages from raw observations.
You’ll learn:

Why voyage reconstruction is hard (the name collision problem)
Schmidt’s four criteria for grouping observations
The haversine formula for calculating distances at sea
How to detect and handle name collisions
Creating voyage summaries with aggregated features




Each ICOADS observation is independent—just a ship ID, position, and timestamp. To reconstruct voyages, we need to connect observations from the same ship in sequence. But there are complications:
Problem 1: No Voyage IDs. Each observation stands alone with no explicit link to consecutive positions. We must infer voyages from patterns in the data.
Problem 2: Multiple Voyages per Ship. Ships made many voyages over years, so the same ship ID appears hundreds of times. We need to separate these into distinct journeys.
Problem 3: Name Collisions (The Hard Part!). Ship IDs are truncated to 9 characters, so different ships can share the same ID. “ELIZABETH” could refer to five different vessels. When we see simultaneous observations at distant locations, we know they must be different ships.



Ben Schmidt developed a robust algorithm that uses four criteria to decide whether two consecutive observations belong to the same voyage:

Same Ship Name. The observations must have the same ID field. This groups observations by vessel identity.
Temporal Continuity (< 30 days). Consecutive observations must be within 30 days of each other. Gaps longer than this indicate separate voyages by the same ship.
Spatial Continuity (< 1000 km). Consecutive observations must be within 1000 km of each other. This prevents impossible jumps caused by data errors or long port stays.
No Simultaneous Observations. If the same ship ID appears in two distant locations on the same day, those observations must come from different physical ships. This criterion handles the name collision problem.






Let’s implement the first two criteria. We’ll work with a small sample dataset first to understand the algorithm, then apply it to the full ICOADS data. The sample below simulates two ships (LOUISVIL and MARYSANN) with observations spanning multiple months.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Simulate some observation data
data = {
    'ID': ['LOUISVIL', 'LOUISVIL', 'LOUISVIL', 'LOUISVIL', 'MARYSANN', 'MARYSANN'],
    'YR': [1840, 1840, 1840, 1841, 1840, 1840],
    'MO': [1, 1, 2, 6, 1, 1],
    'DY': [1, 15, 1, 1, 5, 20],
    'LAT': [37.0, 35.5, 32.0, 38.0, 42.0, 40.5],
    'LON': [-74.0, -72.0, -68.0, -73.0, -70.0, -65.0],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# Create datetime

To apply the spatial continuity criterion, we need to calculate distances between consecutive observations. Since positions are on the surface of a sphere (the Earth), we can’t simply use the Pythagorean theorem. Instead, we use the haversine formula:

def haversine_km(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    """
    Calculate great-circle distance between two points.

    The haversine formula accounts for Earth's curvature.
    Inputs are in decimal degrees; output is in kilometers.
    """
    R = 6371.0  # Earth's radius in kilometers

    # Convert to radians
    lat1_rad = np.radians(lat1)
    lat2_rad = np.radians(lat2)
    dlat = np.radians(lat2 - lat1)
    dlon = np.radians(lon2 - lon1)

    # Haversine formula
    a = np.sin(dlat / 2)**2 + np.cos(lat1_rad) * np.cos(lat2_rad) * np.sin(dlon / 2)**2
    c = 2 * np.arctan2(np.sqrt(a), np.sqrt(1 - a))

    return R * c

::: {.callout-note}
## Why Not Just Use Pythagorean Distance?
On a flat surface, distance = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²). But Earth is a sphere!
At the equator, 1° of longitude ≈ 111 km, but near the poles it approaches 0 km.
The haversine formula accounts for this curvature, giving accurate distances
regardless of latitude.

The trickiest part is handling name collisions—when different physical ships share the same truncated ID. Schmidt’s insight: if the same ID appears in two distant locations on the same day, they must be different ships.

def find_simultaneous_conflicts(df, distance_threshold=500):
    """
    Find days where the same ship ID appears at distant locations.

    This indicates multiple physical ships sharing a truncated name.
    Returns a set of (ID, date) tuples with conflicts.
    """
    conflicts = set()

    # Create date key for grouping
    df = df.copy()
    df['_date_key'] = df['Date'].dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')

    for (ship_id, date_key), group in df.groupby(['ID', '_date_key']):
        if len(group) < 2:
            continue

        # Check if any pair of observations is too far apart
        lats = group['LAT'].values
        lons = group['LON'].values

        for i in range(len(lats)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(lats)):
                dist = haversine_km(lats[i], lons[i], lats[j], lons[j])
                if dist > distance_threshold:
                    conflicts.add((ship_id, date_key))
                    break

    return conflicts

Schmidt’s Key Insight



The 9-character ID truncation means “ELIZABET” could be “Elizabeth”, “Elizabeth Ann”, or “Elizabeth Mary”—completely different ships. But physics helps us: no ship can be in the North Atlantic and South Atlantic on the same day. When we detect impossible simultaneity, we know we’re looking at different vessels sharing a truncated name.











Performance Note



The naive conflict detection below checks every pair of same-day observations—an O(n²) operation. For 1.3 million records, this could be slow. The production script in scripts/reconstruct_voyages.py uses optimizations like early termination and vectorized operations. For learning purposes, the simple version here is clearer.

def reconstruct_voyages(df, max_days=30, max_km=1000, verbose=True):
    """
    Reconstruct voyages using Schmidt's four-criterion algorithm.

    Parameters:
        df: DataFrame with YR, MO, DY, HR, LAT, LON, ID columns
        max_days: Maximum days between consecutive observations
        max_km: Maximum kilometers between consecutive observations
        verbose: Print progress information

    Returns:
        DataFrame with added 'voyage_id' column
    """
    if verbose:
        print(f"Input: {len(df):,} observations, {df['ID'].nunique():,} ship IDs")

    # Create datetime
    df = df.copy()
    df['_yr'] = pd.to_numeric(df['YR'], errors='coerce').fillna(1800).astype(int)
    df['_mo'] = pd.to_numeric(df['MO'], errors='coerce').fillna(1).astype(int).clip(1, 12)
    df['_dy'] = pd.to_numeric(df['DY'], errors='coerce').fillna(1).astype(int).clip(1, 28)

    date_str = (df['_yr'].astype(str) + '-' +
                df['_mo'].astype(str).str.zfill(2) + '-' +
                df['_dy'].astype(str).str.zfill(2))
    df['_datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(date_str, errors='coerce')
    df = df.dropna(subset=['_datetime', 'LAT', 'LON', 'ID'])

    # Sort by ship and time
    df = df.sort_values(['ID', '_datetime']).reset_index(drop=True)

    # Step 1: Find name collisions (criterion 4)
    if verbose:
        print("Detecting name collisions...")
    conflicts = find_simultaneous_conflicts(df)
    if verbose:
        print(f"  Found {len(conflicts)} conflict days")

    # Step 2: Assign voyage IDs
    if verbose:
        print("Assigning voyage IDs...")

    voyage_ids = []
    voyage_counter = 0
    current_voyage = None

    prev_ship = None
    prev_date = None
    prev_lat = None
    prev_lon = None

    for idx, row in df.iterrows():
        ship = row['ID']
        date = row['_datetime']
        lat = row['LAT']
        lon = row['LON']

        start_new_voyage = False

        # Check criterion 1: Same ship
        if ship != prev_ship:
            start_new_voyage = True
        elif prev_date is not None:
            # Check criterion 2: Time gap
            days_gap = (date - prev_date).days
            if days_gap > max_days:
                start_new_voyage = True
            else:
                # Check criterion 3: Distance
                dist = haversine_km(prev_lat, prev_lon, lat, lon)
                if dist > max_km:
                    start_new_voyage = True

        # Check criterion 4: Conflict day for this ship
        date_key = date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
        if (ship, date_key) in conflicts:
            # On conflict days, each observation starts a new voyage
            # (simplified handling)
            start_new_voyage = True

        if start_new_voyage:
            voyage_counter += 1
            current_voyage = f"V{voyage_counter:06d}"

        voyage_ids.append(current_voyage)
        prev_ship = ship
        prev_date = date
        prev_lat = lat
        prev_lon = lon

    df['voyage_id'] = voyage_ids

    if verbose:
        n_voyages = df['voyage_id'].nunique()
        print(f"\nResult: {n_voyages:,} voyages identified")

    return df

Once voyages are identified, we can create summary statistics for each one. These summaries capture the temporal extent (when did the voyage start and end?), spatial extent (where did it go?), and total distance traveled:

def create_voyage_summary(df):
    """
    Create summary statistics for each voyage.

    Returns DataFrame with one row per voyage containing:
    - Temporal extent (start/end dates, duration)
    - Spatial extent (bounding box, mean position)
    - Total distance traveled
    """
    summaries = []

    for vid in df['voyage_id'].unique():
        voyage = df[df['voyage_id'] == vid].sort_values('_datetime')

        summary = {
            'voyage_id': vid,
            'ship_id': voyage['ID'].iloc[0],
            'n_observations': len(voyage),
        }

        # Temporal
        summary['start_date'] = voyage['_datetime'].min()
        summary['end_date'] = voyage['_datetime'].max()
        summary['duration_days'] = (voyage['_datetime'].max() -
                                     voyage['_datetime'].min()).days

        # Spatial
        summary['start_lat'] = voyage['LAT'].iloc[0]
        summary['start_lon'] = voyage['LON'].iloc[0]
        summary['end_lat'] = voyage['LAT'].iloc[-1]
        summary['end_lon'] = voyage['LON'].iloc[-1]
        summary['mean_lat'] = voyage['LAT'].mean()
        summary['mean_lon'] = voyage['LON'].mean()

        # Total distance
        lats = voyage['LAT'].values
        lons = voyage['LON'].values
        total_dist = sum(haversine_km(lats[i-1], lons[i-1], lats[i], lons[i])
                        for i in range(1, len(lats)))
        summary['total_distance_km'] = total_dist

        summaries.append(summary)

    return pd.DataFrame(summaries)

For the next step (machine learning classification), we need to compute spatial profiles for each voyage. A spatial profile divides the world into a grid and records what proportion of a voyage’s observations fell into each cell:

def compute_spatial_profile(voyage_obs, lat_bins=5, lon_bins=5):
    """
    Compute spatial profile: proportion of observations in each grid cell.

    This captures WHERE a voyage spent its time, which differs between
    whaling ships (concentrated in whaling grounds) and merchants
    (following trade routes).
    """
    lat_edges = np.linspace(-90, 90, lat_bins + 1)
    lon_edges = np.linspace(-180, 180, lon_bins + 1)

    # Count observations in each cell
    hist, _, _ = np.histogram2d(
        voyage_obs['LAT'].values,
        voyage_obs['LON'].values,
        bins=[lat_edges, lon_edges]
    )

    # Normalize to proportions
    total = hist.sum()
    if total > 0:
        hist = hist / total

    return hist.flatten()

This matters for classification because whaling ships and merchant ships visit different parts of the ocean. Whalers concentrate in known whaling grounds (Pacific, Arctic, South Atlantic), while merchants follow trade routes between ports. The next notebook uses these profiles to train a classifier.

Schmidt’s four criteria provide a robust way to handle real-world data: same ship ID, temporal continuity (< 30 days), spatial continuity (< 1000 km), and no simultaneous distant observations.
The haversine formula correctly calculates distances on a sphere, which is essential for geographic data.

Questions to Consider




The algorithm uses a 30-day threshold for temporal continuity. What might happen if you set this threshold too low (e.g., 7 days)? What if you set it too high (e.g., 180 days)?
We use a 500 km threshold to detect name collisions (simultaneous observations that are “too far apart”). But sailing ships could cover significant distance in a single day. What’s a reasonable upper bound on how far a 19th-century sailing vessel could travel in 24 hours? Does 500 km seem like a good threshold?
The name collision detection treats each observation on a conflict day as a separate voyage. Can you think of a more sophisticated approach that might correctly group observations from the same physical ship on a conflict day?
Spatial profiles divide the ocean into a grid. What are the tradeoffs between using a coarse grid (5×5) versus a fine grid (50×50)?
This algorithm reconstructs voyages from fragmentary evidence—ship IDs, positions, and timestamps. Historians often face similar challenges when working with incomplete records. What other kinds of historical data might benefit from algorithmic “reconstruction”? (Think about letters, financial records, migration patterns, etc.)
The name collision problem arises because the original record-keepers truncated ship names to save space on punch cards. What does this tell us about how the constraints of one era’s technology can create challenges for future researchers? Can you think of analogous issues with how we store data today?
We’re treating all voyages the same, but a whaling voyage might last 2-3 years while a coastal merchant trip might last 2 weeks. How might you adapt the algorithm to handle such different voyage types? Should you use different thresholds for different kinds of ships?

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
Each ICOADS observation is independent—just a ship ID, position, and timestamp. To reconstruct voyages, we need to connect observations from the same ship in sequence. But there are complications:
Problem 1: No Voyage IDs. Each observation stands alone with no explicit link to consecutive positions. We must infer voyages from patterns in the data.
Problem 2: Multiple Voyages per Ship. Ships made many voyages over years, so the same ship ID appears hundreds of times. We need to separate these into distinct journeys.
Problem 3: Name Collisions (The Hard Part!). Ship IDs are truncated to 9 characters, so different ships can share the same ID. “ELIZABETH” could refer to five different vessels. When we see simultaneous observations at distant locations, we know they must be different ships.

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
Ben Schmidt developed a robust algorithm that uses four criteria to decide whether two consecutive observations belong to the same voyage:

Same Ship Name. The observations must have the same ID field. This groups observations by vessel identity.
Temporal Continuity (< 30 days). Consecutive observations must be within 30 days of each other. Gaps longer than this indicate separate voyages by the same ship.
Spatial Continuity (< 1000 km). Consecutive observations must be within 1000 km of each other. This prevents impossible jumps caused by data errors or long port stays.
No Simultaneous Observations. If the same ship ID appears in two distant locations on the same day, those observations must come from different physical ships. This criterion handles the name collision problem.

                    conflicts.add((ship_id, date_key))
                    break

    return conflicts


# Demonstrate with a conflict scenario
conflict_data = {
    'ID': ['ELIZABET', 'ELIZABET', 'ELIZABET', 'ELIZABET'],
    'YR': [1840, 1840, 1840, 1840],
    'MO': [6, 6, 6, 6],
    'DY': [15, 15, 16, 16],
    'LAT': [40.0, -30.0, 41.0, -28.0],  # Two ships: one in Atlantic, one in S. Pacific
    'LON': [-70.0, -45.0, -68.0, -43.0],
}
df_conflict = pd.DataFrame(conflict_data)
df_conflict['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(df_conflict['YR'].astype(str) + '-' +
                                      df_conflict['MO'].astype(str).str.zfill(2) + '-' +
                                      df_conflict['DY'].astype(str).str.zfill(2))

print("Name Collision Example:")
print("=" * 60)
print(df_conflict.to_string())
print()

# Find conflicts
conflicts = find_simultaneous_conflicts(df_conflict)
print(f"Conflicts detected: {conflicts}")
print()

# Calculate distance between the two June 15 observations
dist = haversine_km(40.0, -70.0, -30.0, -45.0)
print(f"Distance between simultaneous observations: {dist:,.0f} km")
print("This is impossible for one ship → must be two different ELIZABETs!")







Schmidt’s Key Insight



The 9-character ID truncation means “ELIZABET” could be “Elizabeth”, “Elizabeth Ann”, or “Elizabeth Mary”—completely different ships. But physics helps us: no ship can be in the North Atlantic and South Atlantic on the same day. When we detect impossible simultaneity, we know we’re looking at different vessels sharing a truncated name.

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
Performance Note



The naive conflict detection below checks every pair of same-day observations—an O(n²) operation. For 1.3 million records, this could be slow. The production script in scripts/reconstruct_voyages.py uses optimizations like early termination and vectorized operations. For learning purposes, the simple version here is clearer.


Putting it all together:

def reconstruct_voyages(df, max_days=30, max_km=1000, verbose=True):
    """
    Reconstruct voyages using Schmidt's four-criterion algorithm.

    Parameters:
        df: DataFrame with YR, MO, DY, HR, LAT, LON, ID columns
        max_days: Maximum days between consecutive observations
        max_km: Maximum kilometers between consecutive observations
        verbose: Print progress information

    Returns:
        DataFrame with added 'voyage_id' column
    """
    if verbose:
        print(f"Input: {len(df):,} observations, {df['ID'].nunique():,} ship IDs")

    # Create datetime
    df = df.copy()
    df['_yr'] = pd.to_numeric(df['YR'], errors='coerce').fillna(1800).astype(int)
    df['_mo'] = pd.to_numeric(df['MO'], errors='coerce').fillna(1).astype(int).clip(1, 12)
    df['_dy'] = pd.to_numeric(df['DY'], errors='coerce').fillna(1).astype(int).clip(1, 28)

    date_str = (df['_yr'].astype(str) + '-' +
                df['_mo'].astype(str).str.zfill(2) + '-' +
                df['_dy'].astype(str).str.zfill(2))
    df['_datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(date_str, errors='coerce')
    df = df.dropna(subset=['_datetime', 'LAT', 'LON', 'ID'])

    # Sort by ship and time
    df = df.sort_values(['ID', '_datetime']).reset_index(drop=True)

    # Step 1: Find name collisions (criterion 4)
    if verbose:
        print("Detecting name collisions...")
    conflicts = find_simultaneous_conflicts(df)
    if verbose:
        print(f"  Found {len(conflicts)} conflict days")

    # Step 2: Assign voyage IDs
    if verbose:
        print("Assigning voyage IDs...")

    voyage_ids = []
    voyage_counter = 0
    current_voyage = None

    prev_ship = None
    prev_date = None
    prev_lat = None
    prev_lon = None

    for idx, row in df.iterrows():
        ship = row['ID']
        date = row['_datetime']
        lat = row['LAT']
        lon = row['LON']

        start_new_voyage = False

        # Check criterion 1: Same ship
        if ship != prev_ship:
            start_new_voyage = True
        elif prev_date is not None:
            # Check criterion 2: Time gap
            days_gap = (date - prev_date).days
            if days_gap > max_days:
                start_new_voyage = True
            else:
                # Check criterion 3: Distance
                dist = haversine_km(prev_lat, prev_lon, lat, lon)
                if dist > max_km:
                    start_new_voyage = True

        # Check criterion 4: Conflict day for this ship
        date_key = date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
        if (ship, date_key) in conflicts:
            # On conflict days, each observation starts a new voyage
            # (simplified handling)
            start_new_voyage = True

        if start_new_voyage:
            voyage_counter += 1
            current_voyage = f"V{voyage_counter:06d}"

        voyage_ids.append(current_voyage)
        prev_ship = ship
        prev_date = date
        prev_lat = lat
        prev_lon = lon

    df['voyage_id'] = voyage_ids

    if verbose:
        n_voyages = df['voyage_id'].nunique()
        print(f"\nResult: {n_voyages:,} voyages identified")

    return df


# Apply to our sample
print("Full Algorithm Demo:")
print("=" * 60)
df_demo = pd.concat([df[['ID', 'YR', 'MO', 'DY', 'LAT', 'LON']],
                     df_conflict[['ID', 'YR', 'MO', 'DY', 'LAT', 'LON']]])

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
Once voyages are identified, we can create summary statistics for each one. These summaries capture the temporal extent (when did the voyage start and end?), spatial extent (where did it go?), and total distance traveled:

def create_voyage_summary(df):
    """
    Create summary statistics for each voyage.

    Returns DataFrame with one row per voyage containing:
    - Temporal extent (start/end dates, duration)
    - Spatial extent (bounding box, mean position)
    - Total distance traveled
    """
    summaries = []

    for vid in df['voyage_id'].unique():
        voyage = df[df['voyage_id'] == vid].sort_values('_datetime')

        summary = {
            'voyage_id': vid,
            'ship_id': voyage['ID'].iloc[0],
            'n_observations': len(voyage),
        }

        # Temporal
        summary['start_date'] = voyage['_datetime'].min()
        summary['end_date'] = voyage['_datetime'].max()
        summary['duration_days'] = (voyage['_datetime'].max() -
                                     voyage['_datetime'].min()).days

        # Spatial
        summary['start_lat'] = voyage['LAT'].iloc[0]
        summary['start_lon'] = voyage['LON'].iloc[0]
        summary['end_lat'] = voyage['LAT'].iloc[-1]
        summary['end_lon'] = voyage['LON'].iloc[-1]
        summary['mean_lat'] = voyage['LAT'].mean()
        summary['mean_lon'] = voyage['LON'].mean()

        # Total distance
        lats = voyage['LAT'].values
        lons = voyage['LON'].values
        total_dist = sum(haversine_km(lats[i-1], lons[i-1], lats[i], lons[i])
                        for i in range(1, len(lats)))
        summary['total_distance_km'] = total_dist

        summaries.append(summary)

    return pd.DataFrame(summaries)


# Create summaries for our demo
summary_df = create_voyage_summary(df_result)
print("Voyage Summaries:")
print("=" * 60)
print(summary_df.to_string())

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
For the next step (machine learning classification), we need to compute spatial profiles for each voyage. A spatial profile divides the world into a grid and records what proportion of a voyage’s observations fell into each cell:

def compute_spatial_profile(voyage_obs, lat_bins=5, lon_bins=5):
    """
    Compute spatial profile: proportion of observations in each grid cell.

    This captures WHERE a voyage spent its time, which differs between
    whaling ships (concentrated in whaling grounds) and merchants
    (following trade routes).
    """
    lat_edges = np.linspace(-90, 90, lat_bins + 1)
    lon_edges = np.linspace(-180, 180, lon_bins + 1)

    # Count observations in each cell
    hist, _, _ = np.histogram2d(
        voyage_obs['LAT'].values,
        voyage_obs['LON'].values,
        bins=[lat_edges, lon_edges]
    )

    # Normalize to proportions
    total = hist.sum()
    if total > 0:
        hist = hist / total

    return hist.flatten()


# Demo with one voyage
sample_voyage = df_result[df_result['voyage_id'] == 'V000001']
profile = compute_spatial_profile(sample_voyage)

print(f"Voyage V000001: {len(sample_voyage)} observations")
print(f"Profile: {len(profile)} cells (5×5 grid), sum = {profile.sum():.3f}")

The spatial profile is a fingerprint of where a voyage spent its time. A 5×5 grid divides the world’s oceans into 25 cells; the profile records what fraction of observations fell in each cell.
This matters for classification because whaling ships and merchant ships visit different parts of the ocean. Whalers concentrate in known whaling grounds (Pacific, Arctic, South Atlantic), while merchants follow trade routes between ports. The next notebook uses these profiles to train a classifier.

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
Voyage reconstruction is non-trivial because of name collisions and gaps in the data.
Schmidt’s four criteria provide a robust way to handle real-world data: same ship ID, temporal continuity (< 30 days), spatial continuity (< 1000 km), and no simultaneous distant observations.
The haversine formula correctly calculates distances on a sphere, which is essential for geographic data.
Name collisions can be detected when we find impossible simultaneous locations for the same ship ID.
Spatial profiles summarize where a voyage spent its time, preparing the data for machine learning classification.

title: Step 3: Reconstructing Voyages from Observations
text:
With voyages reconstructed, we can move on to more interesting analyses:

Classify voyage types using the spatial patterns we’ve computed (this is the next notebook).
Visualize ship tracks as connected journeys rather than scattered points.
Analyze voyage statistics such as duration, distance, and common routes.







Questions to Consider




The algorithm uses a 30-day threshold for temporal continuity. What might happen if you set this threshold too low (e.g., 7 days)? What if you set it too high (e.g., 180 days)?
We use a 500 km threshold to detect name collisions (simultaneous observations that are “too far apart”). But sailing ships could cover significant distance in a single day. What’s a reasonable upper bound on how far a 19th-century sailing vessel could travel in 24 hours? Does 500 km seem like a good threshold?
The name collision detection treats each observation on a conflict day as a separate voyage. Can you think of a more sophisticated approach that might correctly group observations from the same physical ship on a conflict day?
Spatial profiles divide the ocean into a grid. What are the tradeoffs between using a coarse grid (5×5) versus a fine grid (50×50)?
This algorithm reconstructs voyages from fragmentary evidence—ship IDs, positions, and timestamps. Historians often face similar challenges when working with incomplete records. What other kinds of historical data might benefit from algorithmic “reconstruction”? (Think about letters, financial records, migration patterns, etc.)
The name collision problem arises because the original record-keepers truncated ship names to save space on punch cards. What does this tell us about how the constraints of one era’s technology can create challenges for future researchers? Can you think of analogous issues with how we store data today?
We’re treating all voyages the same, but a whaling voyage might last 2-3 years while a coastal merchant trip might last 2 weeks. How might you adapt the algorithm to handle such different voyage types? Should you use different thresholds for different kinds of ships?

title: Step 4: Classifying Voyage Types with Machine Learning
text:
The Maury collection contains all types of ships—merchants, whalers, naval vessels, passenger ships. To study whaling specifically, we need to identify which voyages were whaling expeditions. This notebook explains Ben Schmidt’s machine learning approach to this classification problem.
You’ll learn:

Why spatial patterns matter for voyage classification
How to create spatial profiles as feature vectors
Why K=3 neighbors (Schmidt’s choice)
The two-pass refinement technique
Visual validation of classification results




Unlike modern datasets with explicit labels, historical records rarely tell us directly what type of ship made each voyage. But different ship types have different spatial signatures:

print("Voyage Types and Their Spatial Patterns:")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
WHALING SHIPS:
  - Concentrate in known whaling grounds
  - Sperm whales: equatorial Pacific
  - Right whales: higher latitudes (40-60°)
  - Long voyages (months to years)
  - Irregular tracks following whale migrations

MERCHANT SHIPS:
  - Follow established trade routes
  - Atlantic crossings: NY ↔ Liverpool, NY ↔ Caribbean
  - Regular, direct paths between ports
  - Shorter voyages (weeks)

NAVAL VESSELS:
  - Patrol coastlines
  - Visit multiple ports in sequence
  - Government expedition patterns

Schmidt's insight: We can LEARN these patterns from a small set of
labeled examples, then classify all voyages automatically.
""")




The key to Schmidt’s method is representing each voyage as a spatial profile: a vector showing what proportion of time was spent in each ocean grid cell.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create a grid dividing the ocean
LAT_BINS = 15  # 12-degree bands
LON_BINS = 15  # 24-degree bands

lat_edges = np.linspace(-90, 90, LAT_BINS + 1)
lon_edges = np.linspace(-180, 180, LON_BINS + 1)

print("Spatial Grid Configuration:")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Latitude bands:  {LAT_BINS} ({180/LAT_BINS:.1f}° each)")
print(f"Longitude bands: {LON_BINS} ({360/LON_BINS:.1f}° each)")
print(f"Total cells:     {LAT_BINS * LON_BINS}")
print()
print("Each voyage becomes a vector of 225 proportions,")
print("one for each grid cell, summing to 1.0")


def create_spatial_profile(lats, lons, lat_edges, lon_edges):
    """
    Create a spatial profile from voyage positions.

    Returns a flattened array of cell proportions.
    """
    # Count observations in each cell
    hist, _, _ = np.histogram2d(lats, lons, bins=[lat_edges, lon_edges])

    # Normalize to proportions
    total = hist.sum()
    if total > 0:
        hist = hist / total

    return hist.flatten()


# Demo with a synthetic whaling voyage (Pacific focus)
np.random.seed(42)
whaling_lats = np.random.normal(0, 15, 100)   # Equatorial
whaling_lons = np.random.normal(-140, 20, 100)  # Pacific

# Demo with a synthetic merchant voyage (Atlantic crossing)
merchant_lats = np.random.normal(40, 5, 50)   # Mid-Atlantic
merchant_lons = np.random.normal(-40, 20, 50)  # Atlantic

profile_whaling = create_spatial_profile(whaling_lats, whaling_lons, lat_edges, lon_edges)
profile_merchant = create_spatial_profile(merchant_lats, merchant_lons, lat_edges, lon_edges)

print("Spatial Profile Comparison:")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Whaling voyage:  {len(profile_whaling)} features, max cell: {profile_whaling.max():.3f}")
print(f"Merchant voyage: {len(profile_merchant)} features, max cell: {profile_merchant.max():.3f}")


# Visualize the profiles
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Reshape for visualization
whaling_grid = profile_whaling.reshape(LAT_BINS, LON_BINS)
merchant_grid = profile_merchant.reshape(LAT_BINS, LON_BINS)

im1 = axes[0].imshow(whaling_grid, origin='lower', aspect='auto',
                      extent=[-180, 180, -90, 90], cmap='Blues')
axes[0].set_title('Whaling Voyage Profile\n(Pacific concentration)')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Longitude')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Latitude')
plt.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[0], label='Proportion')

im2 = axes[1].imshow(merchant_grid, origin='lower', aspect='auto',
                      extent=[-180, 180, -90, 90], cmap='Oranges')
axes[1].set_title('Merchant Voyage Profile\n(Atlantic crossing)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Longitude')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Latitude')
plt.colorbar(im2, ax=axes[1], label='Proportion')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Schmidt used K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) because it’s:

Intuitive: classify based on similar voyages
Non-parametric: no assumptions about data distribution
Interpretable: can examine which voyages are neighbors




print("Schmidt's Choice: K=3")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
Why not K=1?
  - Too sensitive to noise
  - One mislabeled example dominates

Why not K=10 or more?
  - Over-smooths the classification
  - Small but genuine clusters get swamped by majority class
  - Whaling voyages to unusual grounds get misclassified

K=3 balances:
  - Robustness to noise (needs 2/3 agreement)
  - Preserves small clusters
  - Schmidt: "preserves some very small clusters of whaling
    that are nonetheless real"
""")


from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# Create synthetic dataset for demonstration
np.random.seed(42)

# Generate 50 whaling voyages (Pacific-focused)
whaling_profiles = []
for _ in range(50):
    lats = np.random.normal(np.random.uniform(-20, 20), 15, 80)
    lons = np.random.normal(np.random.uniform(-160, -120), 20, 80)
    whaling_profiles.append(create_spatial_profile(lats, lons, lat_edges, lon_edges))

# Generate 50 merchant voyages (Atlantic-focused)
merchant_profiles = []
for _ in range(50):
    lats = np.random.normal(np.random.uniform(30, 50), 8, 40)
    lons = np.random.normal(np.random.uniform(-60, -20), 15, 40)
    merchant_profiles.append(create_spatial_profile(lats, lons, lat_edges, lon_edges))

# Combine into dataset
X = np.array(whaling_profiles + merchant_profiles)
y = ['whaling'] * 50 + ['merchant'] * 50

print("Synthetic Training Dataset:")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Total voyages: {len(y)}")
print(f"Whaling: {sum(1 for label in y if label == 'whaling')}")
print(f"Merchant: {sum(1 for label in y if label == 'merchant')}")
print(f"Features per voyage: {X.shape[1]}")


# Train KNN classifier
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3, weights='distance', metric='euclidean')
knn.fit(X, y)

# Cross-validation to check performance
scores = cross_val_score(knn, X, y, cv=5)
print(f"\nKNN Performance (5-fold CV):")
print(f"  Accuracy: {scores.mean():.1%} ± {scores.std():.1%}")





Schmidt’s key methodological innovation was a two-pass approach:

print("Two-Pass Classification:")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
PASS 1: Initial Classification
  - Train on high-confidence labels only
  - Labels from metadata (whaling ports, ship names)
  - Classify ALL voyages
  - Record prediction confidence

PASS 2: Expanded Training
  - Add high-confidence predictions to training set
  - Retrain with larger dataset
  - Reclassify all voyages
  - Allows discovering patterns not in original metadata

Why it helps:
  - Original labels are sparse (maybe 5% of voyages)
  - Pass 1 finds similar unlabeled voyages
  - Pass 2 uses these to improve classification
  - Can discover whaling voyages from ports without labels
""")


def two_pass_classification(X, initial_labels, k=3, confidence_threshold=0.7):
    """
    Implement Schmidt's two-pass classification.

    Parameters:
        X: Feature matrix (n_samples, n_features)
        initial_labels: Dict mapping sample index to label (sparse)
        k: Number of neighbors
        confidence_threshold: Minimum confidence to add to training

    Returns:
        Final predictions and confidences for all samples
    """
    n_samples = len(X)

    # Build initial training set
    train_indices = list(initial_labels.keys())
    train_labels = [initial_labels[i] for i in train_indices]
    X_train = X[train_indices]

    print(f"Pass 1: Training on {len(train_indices)} labeled samples")

    # First pass
    knn1 = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights='distance')
    knn1.fit(X_train, train_labels)

    # Predict all
    y_pred1 = knn1.predict(X)

    # Get confidence (inverse of distance to neighbors)
    distances, _ = knn1.kneighbors(X)
    mean_dist = distances.mean(axis=1)
    max_dist = mean_dist.max()
    confidence = 1 - (mean_dist / max_dist) if max_dist > 0 else np.ones(n_samples)

    print(f"  Predictions: {sum(y == 'whaling' for y in y_pred1)} whaling, "
          f"{sum(y == 'merchant' for y in y_pred1)} merchant")

    # Second pass: expand training set
    expanded_train_indices = list(train_indices)
    expanded_train_labels = list(train_labels)

    for i in range(n_samples):
        if i not in train_indices and confidence[i] > confidence_threshold:
            expanded_train_indices.append(i)
            expanded_train_labels.append(y_pred1[i])

    n_added = len(expanded_train_indices) - len(train_indices)
    print(f"\nPass 2: Added {n_added} high-confidence predictions")

    # Retrain
    X_train2 = X[expanded_train_indices]
    knn2 = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights='distance')
    knn2.fit(X_train2, expanded_train_labels)

    y_pred2 = knn2.predict(X)
    distances2, _ = knn2.kneighbors(X)
    mean_dist2 = distances2.mean(axis=1)
    max_dist2 = mean_dist2.max()
    confidence2 = 1 - (mean_dist2 / max_dist2) if max_dist2 > 0 else np.ones(n_samples)

    changed = sum(p1 != p2 for p1, p2 in zip(y_pred1, y_pred2))

text:
The key to Schmidt’s method is representing each voyage as a spatial profile: a vector showing what proportion of time was spent in each ocean grid cell.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create a grid dividing the ocean
LAT_BINS = 15  # 12-degree bands
LON_BINS = 15  # 24-degree bands

lat_edges = np.linspace(-90, 90, LAT_BINS + 1)
lon_edges = np.linspace(-180, 180, LON_BINS + 1)

print("Spatial Grid Configuration:")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Latitude bands:  {LAT_BINS} ({180/LAT_BINS:.1f}° each)")
print(f"Longitude bands: {LON_BINS} ({360/LON_BINS:.1f}° each)")
print(f"Total cells:     {LAT_BINS * LON_BINS}")
print()
print("Each voyage becomes a vector of 225 proportions,")
print("one for each grid cell, summing to 1.0")


def create_spatial_profile(lats, lons, lat_edges, lon_edges):
    """
    Create a spatial profile from voyage positions.

    Returns a flattened array of cell proportions.
    """
    # Count observations in each cell
    hist, _, _ = np.histogram2d(lats, lons, bins=[lat_edges, lon_edges])

    # Normalize to proportions
    total = hist.sum()
    if total > 0:
        hist = hist / total

    return hist.flatten()

Schmidt used K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) because it’s:

Intuitive: classify based on similar voyages
Non-parametric: no assumptions about data distribution
Interpretable: can examine which voyages are neighbors




print("Schmidt's Choice: K=3")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
Why not K=1?
  - Too sensitive to noise
  - One mislabeled example dominates

Why not K=10 or more?
  - Over-smooths the classification
  - Small but genuine clusters get swamped by majority class
  - Whaling voyages to unusual grounds get misclassified

K=3 balances:
  - Robustness to noise (needs 2/3 agreement)
  - Preserves small clusters
  - Schmidt: "preserves some very small clusters of whaling
    that are nonetheless real"

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

text:
Schmidt’s key methodological innovation was a two-pass approach:

print("Two-Pass Classification:")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
PASS 1: Initial Classification
  - Train on high-confidence labels only
  - Labels from metadata (whaling ports, ship names)
  - Classify ALL voyages
  - Record prediction confidence

PASS 2: Expanded Training
  - Add high-confidence predictions to training set
  - Retrain with larger dataset
  - Reclassify all voyages
  - Allows discovering patterns not in original metadata

Why it helps:
  - Original labels are sparse (maybe 5% of voyages)
  - Pass 1 finds similar unlabeled voyages
  - Pass 2 uses these to improve classification
  - Can discover whaling voyages from ports without labels
""")


def two_pass_classification(X, initial_labels, k=3, confidence_threshold=0.7):
    """
    Implement Schmidt's two-pass classification.

    Parameters:
        X: Feature matrix (n_samples, n_features)
        initial_labels: Dict mapping sample index to label (sparse)
        k: Number of neighbors
        confidence_threshold: Minimum confidence to add to training

    Returns:
        Final predictions and confidences for all samples
    """
    n_samples = len(X)

    # Build initial training set
    train_indices = list(initial_labels.keys())
    train_labels = [initial_labels[i] for i in train_indices]
    X_train = X[train_indices]

    print(f"Pass 1: Training on {len(train_indices)} labeled samples")

    # First pass
    knn1 = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights='distance')
    knn1.fit(X_train, train_labels)

    # Predict all
    y_pred1 = knn1.predict(X)

    # Get confidence (inverse of distance to neighbors)
    distances, _ = knn1.kneighbors(X)
    mean_dist = distances.mean(axis=1)
    max_dist = mean_dist.max()
    confidence = 1 - (mean_dist / max_dist) if max_dist > 0 else np.ones(n_samples)

    print(f"  Predictions: {sum(y == 'whaling' for y in y_pred1)} whaling, "
          f"{sum(y == 'merchant' for y in y_pred1)} merchant")

    # Second pass: expand training set
    expanded_train_indices = list(train_indices)
    expanded_train_labels = list(train_labels)

    for i in range(n_samples):
        if i not in train_indices and confidence[i] > confidence_threshold:
            expanded_train_indices.append(i)
            expanded_train_labels.append(y_pred1[i])

    n_added = len(expanded_train_indices) - len(train_indices)
    print(f"\nPass 2: Added {n_added} high-confidence predictions")

    # Retrain
    X_train2 = X[expanded_train_indices]
    knn2 = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights='distance')
    knn2.fit(X_train2, expanded_train_labels)

    y_pred2 = knn2.predict(X)
    distances2, _ = knn2.kneighbors(X)
    mean_dist2 = distances2.mean(axis=1)
    max_dist2 = mean_dist2.max()
    confidence2 = 1 - (mean_dist2 / max_dist2) if max_dist2 > 0 else np.ones(n_samples)

    changed = sum(p1 != p2 for p1, p2 in zip(y_pred1, y_pred2))
    print(f"  Predictions changed: {changed}")
    print(f"  Final: {sum(y == 'whaling' for y in y_pred2)} whaling, "
          f"{sum(y == 'merchant' for y in y_pred2)} merchant")

    return y_pred2, confidence2

text:
About This Project
I’ve been teaching with Ben Schmidt’s classic digital history blog series on mapping whaling voyages for well over a decade. They provide arresting visuals of the history of American whaling voyages alongside a series of interesting methodological reflections on how to use quantitative data effectively in historical practice. However, they were written in a moment when sharing code and data was harder than it is today, and the lack of those artifacts has limited how students can engage with the material.
As we move into the second quarter of the twenty-first century, data has generally become easier to find, code has become easier to share, and new data formats have made it easier to perform calculations that were prohibitively difficult 14 years ago.
The project you are reading attempts attempts to reconstruct Schmidt’s full pipeline, using modern Python libraries that can run on a well-provisioned laptop. In a series of discrete steps, we: - locate the dataset in its current location - extract the relevant records using the method that Schmidt describes - take advantage of major advances in data storage & rewrite the dataset to Parquet format - explore Schmidt’s method for classifying voyages, as well as some alternative methods - mimic his static visualizations, and - use modern open source mapping tools to imitate the complex voyage animations which made the blog so popular a decade and a half ago - TODO: I also hope to discuss and implement some enhancements to Schmidt’s work, when I get the time.
The project can be read here, on the web, but it’s also possible to run all of the code locally as a set of Jupyter notebooks. I hope the multiple formats help you engage with the project in different ways: passively reading for those with less time or technical skill, active tinkering for those with more.
Either way, by following along you’ll learn to:

Download raw logbook data from NOAA’s ICOADS archive
Parse the cryptic IMMA1 fixed-width format into modern data structures
Reconstruct individual ship voyages from scattered observations
Classify voyages as whaling or merchant ships using machine learning
Visualize the results with animated “ghost ship” maps

Before you begin, you should read through Schmidt’s whole series of posts. A suggested order is: - Reading digital sources: a case study in ship’s logs, an overview of the whole project. - Data Narratives and Structural History, an introduction to the main arguments about how to do history with data - You can probably skip Melville Plots, though if you’re interested in Melville for other reasons this post has a few good tidbits, - Machine learning at sea, the most direct discussion of his classification technique, - When you have a MALLET, a critique of topic modelling, - Where are the individuals, a metahistorical reflection, and finally - Reading Digital Sources, a synopsis of the series.
We won’t address all the questions he raises in the series, but his reflections will help make sense of the steps we’re taking.

The Data: Maury Collection (ICOADS Deck 701)






Who Was Matthew Maury?



Matthew Fontaine Maury (1806-1873) was something of a data pioneer, and generally thought of as a founder of oceanography. For almost twenty years, he systematically collecting ship logbooks from captains worldwide. His synthesis of thousands of voyages created the first wind and current charts, with numerous practical benefits for sailors, and scientific benefits for future generations of oceanographers and climate scientists.
Maury’s Wikipedia page


The Maury Collection contains approximately 1.3 million observations from over 13,700 voyages between 1795 and 1861. Each observation records:

Position: Latitude and longitude
Date/Time: Year, month, day, hour
Weather: Wind direction/speed, barometric pressure, air/sea temperature
Ship identity: Partial ship names, voyage identifiers

As Schmidt notes, the original hand-written logs were much more complex than the records that survive today. We’ll talk more about that in the next section.

title: Step 2: Converting IMMA1 to Parquet Format
text:
This notebook explains how to convert the downloaded IMMA1 data to Apache Parquet, a modern columnar format optimized for analytical queries. You’ll learn:

Why fixed-width formats exist and their historical context
How to parse IMMA1 fields including coordinate encoding
What columnar storage means and why it matters
How Parquet achieves 37× compression on our data




The IMMA1 (International Maritime Meteorological Archive) format dates from the era of punch cards and magnetic tape. While it has served well for archival purposes, modern analysis benefits from formats designed for today’s tools.


In fixed-width formats, each field occupies specific character positions in every line:

# A sample IMMA1 record
sample = "1840 1 1     3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1"

print("Fixed-Width Format Example:")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Record: '{sample[:50]}...'")
print()
print("Position | Value | Meaning")
print("-" * 40)
print(f"  0-4    | '{sample[0:4]}'  | Year")
print(f"  4-6    | '{sample[4:6]}'  | Month")
print(f"  6-8    | '{sample[6:8]}'  | Day")
print(f" 12-17   | '{sample[12:17]}' | Latitude (×100)")
print(f" 17-23   | '{sample[17:23]}'| Longitude (×100)")
print(f" 35-44   | '{sample[35:44]}'| Ship ID")

Advantages in the punch card era: - No delimiters needed (saves space) - Easy to read specific columns from tape - Self-documenting if you know the schema
Disadvantages for modern analysis: - Must read entire records even if you need one field - Everything is text (no native numbers) - No compression - Requires custom parsers



We can convert fixed-width data to CSV (Comma-Separated Values), a more widely-supported format.
Here are our three sample IMMA1 records:
1840 1 1     3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL
1840 1 2     3810 28720 13 4    10LOUISVIL
1840 1 3     3650 28410 13 4    10LOUISVIL
After parsing the fixed positions and converting coordinates (divide by 100, subtract 360 for west longitudes), we get this table:

1840,1,3,36.50,-75.90,LOUISVIL
CSV is a row-based storage format—each line contains all fields for one observation, separated by commas. While CSV is more portable than fixed-width:

Pro: Human-readable delimiters, widely supported by all tools
Pro: Self-describing headers
Con: Still stores data row-by-row (inefficient for column operations)
Con: No native types (everything is text)
Con: Poor compression (similar values scattered across rows)

For analytical workloads, we need something better: columnar storage.



Apache Parquet stores data by column rather than by row:
Row-based (IMMA1, CSV):
  Record 1: 1840, 1, 1, 37.02, -73.95, LOUISVIL, ...
  Record 2: 1840, 1, 2, 38.10, -72.80, LOUISVIL, ...
  Record 3: 1840, 1, 3, 36.50, -74.10, LOUISVIL, ...

Columnar (Parquet):
  Year column:  [1840, 1840, 1840, ...]
  Month column: [1, 1, 1, ...]
  Day column:   [1, 2, 3, ...]
  Lat column:   [37.02, 38.10, 36.50, ...]
  Lon column:   [-73.95, -72.80, -74.10, ...]
  Ship column:  [LOUISVIL, LOUISVIL, LOUISVIL, ...]
Why columnar is better for analysis:

Similar values together → excellent compression
Read only needed columns → faster queries
Type-specific encoding → efficient storage
Vectorized operations → CPU optimization

Latitude and longitude use a special encoding that requires careful parsing. We’ll write a python conversion to convert to familiar units:

def parse_lat(raw_value):
    """
    Parse IMMA1 latitude field.

    Format: Signed integer, scaled by 100.
    Example: 3702 → 37.02°N, -2190 → 21.90°S
    """
    if not raw_value or not raw_value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        raw = int(raw_value)
        return raw / 100.0  # Divide by 100 to get decimal degrees
    except ValueError:
        return None


def parse_lon(raw_value):
    """
    Parse IMMA1 longitude field.

    Format: Integer scaled by 100, with special encoding for west.
    - Values 0-18000: 0° to 180°E
    - Values > 18000: West longitudes stored as (360 + lon) × 100

    Example: 28605 → 286.05 → 286.05 - 360 = -73.95°W
    """
    if not raw_value or not raw_value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        raw = int(raw_value)
        lon = raw / 100.0
        if lon > 180:
            lon = lon - 360  # Convert to negative (west) longitude
        return lon
    except ValueError:
        return None

for lat_raw, lon_raw, description in test_cases:

    lon = parse_lon(lon_raw)
    print(f"\n{description}:")

    print(f"  Decoded: {lat:.2f}°, {lon:.2f}°")




Meteorological fields also need a conversion function:

def parse_scaled_field(value, scale=10):
    """
    Parse a scaled numeric field.

    Many IMMA1 fields store values multiplied by 10 to avoid decimals.
    Example: Temperature 235 → 23.5°C
    """
    if not value or not value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        return int(value) / scale
    except ValueError:
        return None

Here’s the full record parsing function. It’s long because each field needs to be handled explicitly:

def parse_imma1_line(line):
    """
    Parse a single IMMA1 record into a dictionary.

    Returns a dict with all extracted fields, properly typed.
    """
    record = {}

    # Date/time fields
    record['YR'] = line[0:4].strip() or None
    record['MO'] = line[4:6].strip() or None
    record['DY'] = line[6:8].strip() or None

    # Hour (stored as HHMM, convert to decimal hours)
    hr_raw = line[8:12].strip()
    if hr_raw:
        try:
            record['HR'] = int(hr_raw) / 100.0
        except ValueError:
            record['HR'] = None
    else:
        record['HR'] = None

    # Position with correct parsing
    record['LAT'] = parse_lat(line[12:17])
    record['LON'] = parse_lon(line[17:23])

    # Ship identification
    record['ID'] = line[35:44].strip() or None

    # Sea level pressure (tenths of hPa)
    slp_raw = line[62:67].strip()
    record['SLP'] = parse_scaled_field(slp_raw) if slp_raw else None

    # Air temperature (tenths of °C)
    at_raw = line[72:76].strip()
    record['AT'] = parse_scaled_field(at_raw) if at_raw else None

    # Sea surface temperature (tenths of °C)
    sst_raw = line[87:91].strip()
    record['SST'] = parse_scaled_field(sst_raw) if sst_raw else None

    # Deck number from C1 attachment
    if len(line) > 124:
        record['DCK'] = line[118:121].strip() or None
    else:
        record['DCK'] = None

    return record


# Demonstrate parsing
sample_line = "1840 1 1 1200 3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685              10132   235           182                     165 20673701 69 5 0 1"
parsed = parse_imma1_line(sample_line)

print("Parsed Record:")
print("=" * 60)
for key, value in parsed.items():
    if value is not None:
        print(f"  {key:6}: {value}")







If you’re completely new to Python, you may never have seen pandas before. It’s the most important library for doing data science in Python. A DataFrame is essentially a table—rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or SQL table—but with powerful built-in methods for filtering, grouping, and transforming data. The pattern df = pd.DataFrame(some_data) converts a list of dictionaries (or other data structures) into a DataFrame you can manipulate. By convention, we use df as a variable name for DataFrames.

import pandas as pd

# Simulate reading multiple records
sample_records = [
    parse_imma1_line("1840 1 1 1200 3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685              10132   235           182                     165 20673701 69 5 0 1"),
    parse_imma1_line("1840 1 2 0800 3810 28720 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685              10145   220           178                     165 20673701 69 5 0 1"),
    parse_imma1_line("1840 1 3 1600 3650 28410 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685              10098   245           185                     165 20673701 69 5 0 1"),
]

df_sample = pd.DataFrame(sample_records)

print("Sample DataFrame:")
print("=" * 60)
print(df_sample.to_string())
print()
print("Data Types:")
print(df_sample.dtypes)




Writing a DataFrame to Parquet is a single line. Let’s write our sample data to a real file:

from pathlib import Path

# Ensure output directory exists
Path('output').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Write with Snappy compression (the default, fast and good compression)
df_sample.to_parquet('output/sample_records.parquet', engine='pyarrow', compression='snappy')

print(f"Wrote {len(df_sample)} records to output/sample_records.parquet")




Let’s read it back and compare file sizes:

import os

# Read the Parquet file back
df_read = pd.read_parquet('output/sample_records.parquet')

# Check the data matches
print("Roundtrip verification:")
print(f"  Records written: {len(df_sample)}")
print(f"  Records read:    {len(df_read)}")
print(f"  Data matches:    {df_sample.equals(df_read)}")

# Compare to equivalent CSV

parquet_size = os.path.getsize('output/sample_records.parquet')
csv_size = os.path.getsize('output/sample_records.csv')

print(f"\nFile sizes:")
print(f"  CSV:     {csv_size:,} bytes")
print(f"  Parquet: {parquet_size:,} bytes")
print(f"  Ratio:   {csv_size / parquet_size:.1f}x smaller")







Note



With only 3 records, Parquet’s overhead makes it larger than CSV. The compression benefits appear with larger datasets—at 1.3 million records, we see 37× compression.






On the full Maury dataset:

Size
Notes

~15 MB

Compression ratio: 37×
Why so much compression?

Columnar layout groups similar values
Run-length encoding for repeated values
Dictionary encoding for ship IDs
Delta encoding for sorted columns
Snappy compression on top




One of Parquet’s key advantages is reading only the columns you need:
# Load everything
df_full = pd.read_parquet('data/icoads_deck701_maury.parquet')
# → Loads all 30+ columns, uses ~200MB memory

# Load only positions
df_positions = pd.read_parquet(
    'data/icoads_deck701_maury.parquet',
    columns=['YR', 'LAT', 'LON']
)
# → Loads 3 columns, uses ~30MB memory, 5× faster

# Load with filtering (requires pyarrow filters)
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
table = pq.read_table(
    'data/icoads_deck701_maury.parquet',
    columns=['LAT', 'LON', 'SST'],
    filters=[('YR', '>=', '1840'), ('YR', '<', '1850')]
)
# → Only reads 1840s data from disk



Now let’s convert the complete ICOADS dataset. The full file has ~1.3 million records, so we’ll process it in chunks to avoid running out of memory.






Memory Management with Chunks



When processing large files, we can’t load everything into memory at once. Instead, we:

Read a “chunk” of records (e.g., 100,000 at a time)
Convert that chunk to Parquet format
Append it to the output file
Repeat until done

PyArrow’s ParquetWriter handles the appending automatically.




First, let’s define our input/output paths and verify the input file exists:

from pathlib import Path
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# File paths
input_file = Path('data/icoads_deck701_maury.imma')
output_file = Path('data/icoads_deck701_maury.parquet')

# Verify input exists
if input_file.exists():
    input_size_mb = input_file.stat().st_size / 1024 / 1024
    print(f"Input file: {input_file}")
    print(f"Size: {input_size_mb:.1f} MB")
else:
    print(f"Input file not found: {input_file}")
    print("Run the download script first: uv run python scripts/download_icoads_deck701.py")




Counting records first lets us show progress. This takes a few seconds on a large file:

# Count lines for progress reporting
total_records = sum(1 for _ in open(input_file))
print(f"Total records: {total_records:,}")




Here’s the core conversion loop. We read the file line by line, parse each record, and write to Parquet in batches:

chunk_size = 100_000  # Records per chunk
records = []
records_processed = 0
writer = None

with open(input_file, 'r', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace') as f:
    for line in f:
        line = line.rstrip('\n\r')
        if not line:
            continue

        # Parse the IMMA1 record (using our function from earlier)
        record = parse_imma1_line(line)
        records.append(record)
        records_processed += 1

        # When chunk is full, write to Parquet
        if len(records) >= chunk_size:
            df_chunk = pd.DataFrame(records)
            table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df_chunk)

            # Create writer on first chunk (to capture schema)
            if writer is None:
                writer = pq.ParquetWriter(output_file, table.schema, compression='snappy')

            writer.write_table(table)
            records = []  # Clear for next chunk

            print(f"Processed {records_processed:,} records...")

# Don't forget the final partial chunk!
if records:
    df_chunk = pd.DataFrame(records)
    table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df_chunk)
    if writer is None:
        writer = pq.ParquetWriter(output_file, table.schema, compression='snappy')
    writer.write_table(table)

# Close the writer
if writer:
    writer.close()

print(f"\nConversion complete: {records_processed:,} records")







Don’t Forget the Final Chunk!



A common bug is forgetting to write the last partial chunk after the loop ends. If your file has 1,350,000 records and your chunk size is 100,000, the last 50,000 records would be lost without the final if records: block.






# Check output file
output_size_mb = output_file.stat().st_size / 1024 / 1024
compression_ratio = input_size_mb / output_size_mb

print(f"Output file: {output_file}")
print(f"Size: {output_size_mb:.1f} MB")
print(f"Compression ratio: {compression_ratio:.1f}x")

# Quick sanity check
df_check = pd.read_parquet(output_file, columns=['YR', 'LAT', 'LON'])
print(f"\nRecords in Parquet: {len(df_check):,}")
print(f"Year range: {df_check['YR'].min()} - {df_check['YR'].max()}")




If you prefer to run the conversion in the background without stepping through the notebook, use the command-line script:

Options:

-i custom_input.imma: Specify input file
-o custom_output.parquet: Specify output file
--chunk-size 50000: Reduce chunk size for memory-constrained systems

Expected results:

Input: data/icoads_deck701_maury.imma (567 MB)
Output: data/icoads_deck701_maury.parquet (15 MB)
Compression ratio: 37×





With the data in Parquet format, we can efficiently:

Reconstruct voyages from individual observations (next notebook)
Classify voyage types using machine learning
Create visualizations of maritime traffic patterns





IMMA1 is a fixed-width format from the punch card era
Coordinates require special parsing: divide by 100, subtract 360 for west longitudes
Parquet stores data by column enabling selective reading and excellent compression

title: Step 2: Converting IMMA1 to Parquet Format
text:
The IMMA1 (International Maritime Meteorological Archive) format dates from the era of punch cards and magnetic tape. While it has served well for archival purposes, modern analysis benefits from formats designed for today’s tools.


In fixed-width formats, each field occupies specific character positions in every line:

# A sample IMMA1 record
sample = "1840 1 1     3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1"

print("Fixed-Width Format Example:")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Record: '{sample[:50]}...'")
print()
print("Position | Value | Meaning")
print("-" * 40)
print(f"  0-4    | '{sample[0:4]}'  | Year")
print(f"  4-6    | '{sample[4:6]}'  | Month")
print(f"  6-8    | '{sample[6:8]}'  | Day")
print(f" 12-17   | '{sample[12:17]}' | Latitude (×100)")
print(f" 17-23   | '{sample[17:23]}'| Longitude (×100)")
print(f" 35-44   | '{sample[35:44]}'| Ship ID")

Advantages in the punch card era: - No delimiters needed (saves space) - Easy to read specific columns from tape - Self-documenting if you know the schema
Disadvantages for modern analysis: - Must read entire records even if you need one field - Everything is text (no native numbers) - No compression - Requires custom parsers



We can convert fixed-width data to CSV (Comma-Separated Values), a more widely-supported format.
Here are our three sample IMMA1 records:

1840 1 2     3810 28720 13 4    10LOUISVIL
1840 1 3     3650 28410 13 4    10LOUISVIL

1840,1,3,36.50,-75.90,LOUISVIL
CSV is a row-based storage format—each line contains all fields for one observation, separated by commas. While CSV is more portable than fixed-width:

Pro: Human-readable delimiters, widely supported by all tools
Pro: Self-describing headers
Con: Still stores data row-by-row (inefficient for column operations)
Con: No native types (everything is text)
Con: Poor compression (similar values scattered across rows)

For analytical workloads, we need something better: columnar storage.



Apache Parquet stores data by column rather than by row:
Row-based (IMMA1, CSV):
  Record 1: 1840, 1, 1, 37.02, -73.95, LOUISVIL, ...
  Record 2: 1840, 1, 2, 38.10, -72.80, LOUISVIL, ...
  Record 3: 1840, 1, 3, 36.50, -74.10, LOUISVIL, ...

Columnar (Parquet):
  Year column:  [1840, 1840, 1840, ...]
  Month column: [1, 1, 1, ...]
  Day column:   [1, 2, 3, ...]
  Lat column:   [37.02, 38.10, 36.50, ...]
  Lon column:   [-73.95, -72.80, -74.10, ...]
  Ship column:  [LOUISVIL, LOUISVIL, LOUISVIL, ...]
Why columnar is better for analysis:

Similar values together → excellent compression
Read only needed columns → faster queries
Type-specific encoding → efficient storage
Vectorized operations → CPU optimization

Latitude and longitude use a special encoding that requires careful parsing. We’ll write a python conversion to convert to familiar units:

def parse_lat(raw_value):
    """
    Parse IMMA1 latitude field.

    Format: Signed integer, scaled by 100.
    Example: 3702 → 37.02°N, -2190 → 21.90°S
    """
    if not raw_value or not raw_value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        raw = int(raw_value)
        return raw / 100.0  # Divide by 100 to get decimal degrees
    except ValueError:
        return None


def parse_lon(raw_value):
    """
    Parse IMMA1 longitude field.

    Format: Integer scaled by 100, with special encoding for west.
    - Values 0-18000: 0° to 180°E
    - Values > 18000: West longitudes stored as (360 + lon) × 100

    Example: 28605 → 286.05 → 286.05 - 360 = -73.95°W
    """
    if not raw_value or not raw_value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        raw = int(raw_value)
        lon = raw / 100.0
        if lon > 180:
            lon = lon - 360  # Convert to negative (west) longitude
        return lon
    except ValueError:
        return None


# Demonstrate coordinate parsing
print("Coordinate Parsing Examples:")

    ("-2190", "5377", "South Atlantic"),
    ("4520", "12350", "Mediterranean"),
]

for lat_raw, lon_raw, description in test_cases:
    lat = parse_lat(lat_raw)

    print(f"  Decoded: {lat:.2f}°, {lon:.2f}°")

def parse_scaled_field(value, scale=10):
    """
    Parse a scaled numeric field.

    Many IMMA1 fields store values multiplied by 10 to avoid decimals.
    Example: Temperature 235 → 23.5°C
    """
    if not value or not value.strip():
        return None
    try:
        return int(value) / scale
    except ValueError:
        return None

Here’s the full record parsing function. It’s long because each field needs to be handled explicitly:

def parse_imma1_line(line):
    """
    Parse a single IMMA1 record into a dictionary.

    Returns a dict with all extracted fields, properly typed.
    """
    record = {}

    # Date/time fields
    record['YR'] = line[0:4].strip() or None
    record['MO'] = line[4:6].strip() or None
    record['DY'] = line[6:8].strip() or None

    # Hour (stored as HHMM, convert to decimal hours)
    hr_raw = line[8:12].strip()
    if hr_raw:
        try:
            record['HR'] = int(hr_raw) / 100.0
        except ValueError:
            record['HR'] = None
    else:
        record['HR'] = None

    # Position with correct parsing
    record['LAT'] = parse_lat(line[12:17])
    record['LON'] = parse_lon(line[17:23])

    # Ship identification
    record['ID'] = line[35:44].strip() or None

    # Sea level pressure (tenths of hPa)
    slp_raw = line[62:67].strip()
    record['SLP'] = parse_scaled_field(slp_raw) if slp_raw else None

    # Air temperature (tenths of °C)
    at_raw = line[72:76].strip()
    record['AT'] = parse_scaled_field(at_raw) if at_raw else None

    # Sea surface temperature (tenths of °C)
    sst_raw = line[87:91].strip()
    record['SST'] = parse_scaled_field(sst_raw) if sst_raw else None

    # Deck number from C1 attachment
    if len(line) > 124:
        record['DCK'] = line[118:121].strip() or None
    else:
        record['DCK'] = None

    return record

sample_line = "1840 1 1 1200 3702 28605 13 4    10LOUISVIL   1 685              10132   235           182                     165 20673701 69 5 0 1"
parsed = parse_imma1_line(sample_line)

print("Parsed Record:")
print("=" * 60)
for key, value in parsed.items():
    if value is not None:
        print(f"  {key:6}: {value}")
